input:
## Case
The fleet is now due for renewal, and it is important to note that the vehicles currently in service are approaching the end of their working lives at broadly the same time, which means that the replacement decision cannot simply be deferred on a vehicle-by-vehicle basis. Electrification is the candidate replacement under consideration: battery electric vehicles charged at the depots where the fleet is based overnight. The case for this approach rests on three main grounds. Firstly, running costs favour the electric vehicle on the duties the fleet actually works, which are short, repeated routes returning to base; fuel is presently bought per vehicle under the existing arrangement, whereas depot charging draws on the site supply that the firm already pays for. Secondly, maintenance is considerably simpler on the electric drivetrain, with fewer wearing parts in regular service, reducing both downtime and workshop burden. Thirdly, the fleet's operating area is subject to tightening emissions requirements, which a diesel replacement would meet only partially and for a limited period, underscoring the risk of investing in a technology that is already being regulated away. It should be emphasised that the proposal does not claim that electrification suits every vehicle in the fleet: duties that run long distances from base, or that cannot return for charging, are held out of the first stage and will be reviewed once the depot-based vehicles are successfully in service.

## Costs
The capital cost of the programme is $1749k. This comprehensive figure covers the vehicles themselves, the charging points at the depots, and the electrical works needed to supply them. The appraisal horizon is 15 years, matching the expected service life of both the vehicles and the charging installation. Operating costs are not stated as a single figure at this stage, since electricity for charging, maintenance, and the residual value of the vehicles at the end of the horizon all carry uncertainty that the detailed design stage is specifically intended to narrow down. The capital figure of $1749k is therefore the commitment that this proposal asks the firm to plan against, and the appraisal compares it with the cost of a like-for-like diesel replacement over exactly the same horizon and on exactly the same basis, thereby ensuring that the two routes are judged on a fully equal footing. No contractor is named in this proposal, and no supply price is treated as settled; the figures presented are planning figures in support of the decision requested below.

## Schedule
Work will start one quarter after approval has been granted. The first stage is detailed design, encompassing vehicle selection against the fleet's actual duty records, charging layout at each depot, and the connection works to be agreed with the supply provider. Procurement follows on from design, and vehicles will be exchanged as the present fleet reaches its planned withdrawal dates rather than in a single disruptive changeover, so that operations can continue smoothly throughout the transition and charging capacity is commissioned well ahead of the vehicles that depend on it. Depots will take the vehicles in sequence, and each depot's charging installation will be fully complete before its first electric vehicles arrive on site. The design stage will also confirm the order in which duties transfer, with the most regular and shortest rounds moving first in order to build an operating record for the later stages, and the transition period will run both vehicle types side by side at the depots. The schedule deliberately carries no fixed calendar dates beyond the start, because the precise sequence depends on the withdrawal dates that will be set during detailed design.

## Decision requested
The decision requested at this stage is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to construction. Approval commits the firm to the design work and to nothing further at this point: the vehicle purchases, the charging installation, and the electrical works will each return for a separate decision once detailed design has fixed their scope and prices. The design stage will settle the key questions that this proposal leaves open, namely which vehicles are to be replaced first, what charging capacity each depot requires, and what the connection works will involve in practice. If detailed design subsequently shows the capital cost moving materially from the figure set out in the costs section, the proposal will return for further consideration before any construction commitment whatsoever is made.
